Subject: Performance SLO follow-up: context window, tokens, and latency impact

Hi Syd / FinCo team,

Thanks again for taking the time yesterday — great conversation. Quick recap and action items so we can align on the SLOs and next technical steps: 

- Target latency SLOs: 95th percentile <= 400ms for single-turn chat (customer requirement), but you said some flows can tolerate up to 800ms.
- Throughput expectations: approx 60 qps peak for inference requests (mostly short prompts).
- Concurrency: you expect spikes to ~300 concurrent connections during batch runs.
- Streaming: streaming responses preferred for multi-turn assistant UX (we discussed chunked tokens every ~250ms).
- Context window: you mentioned needing ~32k context for user history + documents in some cases; typical requests will be 8k tokens.

Next steps (owner in parentheses):
1) We’ll run a quick latency stress test based on your 8k/32k distributions and share results (Rishi).
2) Confirm whether 95th pctl across peak or sustained traffic matters more (Syd).
3) If streaming is required, we’ll validate streaming latency and token flush behavior (Marissa + Rishi).

I’ve attached the draft latency test plan and a short worksheet — please flag anything missing.

Thanks,
Marissa
Director, Sales (Platform)
Redwood Inference

Thanks Marissa — helpful summary. A few clarifications from our side: 

- 95th pctl should be measured during peak sustained traffic (so include the 60 qps sustained with spikes to 90 qps for short windows).
- For the 32k context case: this is only for archival search + long multi-turn threads (~10% of requests). Most traffic is indeed ~8k tokens.
- Streaming is important for the agent UX; ideally initial partial responses should stream within 250–300ms for short prompts (<2k tokens). For long context (32k), acceptable streaming start may be slower but should still produce first chunk <800ms.
- Concurrency: spikes to 300 are short (a few minutes) but we want graceful degradation rather than hard failures.

Can Rishi share what config changes (batching, KV cache, quantization) we should expect to tune to meet these? Also confirm whether your hosted API has pinned capacity options that align with these SLOs.

—Syd
VP Product, FinCo
From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>
To: Syd Prakash <syd.prakash@finco.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>

Date: Mon, 06 Jul 2026 15:20:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Performance SLO follow-up: context window, tokens, and latency impact

Hi Syd — thanks, this is great context. TL;DR: We can meet the 95p<=400ms for the common 8k requests with the right profile; 32k requests will need different tradeoffs. Details below.

1) Single-turn / 8k requests (most traffic)
- With a standard FP16 model profile + moderate batching (batch sizes 4–8) on our Dedicated/Hosted with reserved pools, we've seen 95p latencies in the 250–380ms range at 60 qps.
- KV caching for repeated prefixes will reduce compute by ~15–25% depending on hit rate — helpful for chat where users re-use system prompts.

2) Streaming expectations
- For short prompts (<2k tokens), streaming start within 250–300ms is realistic if we:
  a) enable prefix caching,
  b) set aggressive flush thresholds for first token (send immediately once ready), and
  c) avoid large batch aggregation for low-latency routes (route these to low-latency nodes).
- For 32k context cases, the initial token generation latency will be dominated by encoder/attention cost across the long sequence; expect first-chunk times ~600–900ms without additional engineering (longer if quantized kernels slower at very long sequences). We can optimize with:
  - Sparse attention or chunked encoding where applicable,
  - Pre-warming KV cache for retrieved docs, and
  - Dedicated nodes with larger memory / optimized kernels for long-context models.

3) 32k context and throughput tradeoffs
- Serving 32k windows increases per-request compute and memory; throughput at equivalent latency drops significantly (we measure ~3–6x slower per token on current kernels for 32k vs 8k depending on model).
- Options:
  a) keep model with 32k and accept higher latency for those 10% of requests; use async processing + streaming for UX,
  b) summarize / compress context to shorter retrieval context before sending (we've seen 4–8x effective latency improvement), or
  c) use a hybrid where long-context requests route to a dedicated long-window pool with reserved capacity and higher cost.

4) Concurrency and graceful degradation
- For short spikes to 300 concurrent connections, autoscaling + burst capacity helps but cold-starts can increase p95; recommend a small reserved buffer for the long-window pool and burstable Dedicated capacity for short spikes.

5) Quantization and kernel tradeoffs
- Int8/4-bit quantization reduces memory and increases throughput but sometimes increases variance in token latency for long contexts due to different kernel paths. We'll validate on your model(s).

6) Proposed immediate tests (we can run these in 48–72 hours)
- Baseline 8k token latency test at 60 qps sustained + 90 qps 2-min spike (measure p50/p95/p99).
- Streaming start latency for <2k and 8k prompts.
- 32k workload test at 10 qps and concurrency profile to measure tail latency and throughput.

I’ve attached a quick test plan and can start runs once you confirm the model variant and whether summarization is acceptable for long-context flows.

—Rishi
Sr. Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
